extracted.intended_audience: writers, literature students, and general readers learning about narrative point of view
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on using first-person point of view in storytelling: what counts as first-person, its forms and styles, narrator identities, reliability issues, and medium-specific considerations (e.g., film voice-over).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of first-person grammar / point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: A first-person narrative (also known as a first-person perspective, voice, point of view, etc.) is a mode of storytelling in which a storyteller recounts events from that storyteller's own personal point of view, using first-person grammar such as "I", "me", "my", and "myself" (also, in plural form, "we", "us", etc.). It must be narrated by a first-person character, such as a protagonist (or other focal character), re-teller, witness, or peripheral character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the defining requirement: the narrator must speak in first person. Examples: Jane Eyre (protagonist narrator), Srikanta. Use first-person grammar consistently unless deliberately shifting point of view for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited perspective / knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: This device allows the audience to see the narrator's mind's eye view of the fictional universe, but it is limited to the narrator's experiences and awareness of the true state of affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect gaps and blind spots: the narrator cannot reliably describe events they did not witness or understand. Authors may broaden the reader's knowledge by relaying dialogue or reported information, or by switching narrators to other characters when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator identity (major/minor/frame/focal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A story written in the first person is most often told by the main character, but may also be told from the perspective of a less important character as they witness events, or a person retelling a story they were told by someone else. These can be distinguished as 'first-person major' or 'first-person minor' points of view. Frame narrators report others' narratives at one or more removes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the narrator role to shape what the reader can know and feel: principal (e.g., Gulliver), close observer (Dr. Watson), or peripheral/focal observer (Nick Carraway). Frame narrators (e.g., Mr. Lockwood in Wuthering Heights) can add layers and distance; identify explicitly if you use a frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability / unreliable narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person narration presents the narrative through the perspective of a particular character. The narrator is an imperfect witness by definition... they may be pursuing some hidden agenda (an 'unreliable narrator').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider sources of unreliability: ignorance, bias, poor insight, character flaws (tardiness, cowardice), sensory limitations (poor eyesight), elapsed time since events, and motivation for telling (confession, self-justification, entertainment). Use unreliability intentionally to create ambiguity or subvert reader expectations; make clear why/when the narrator might mislead or lack information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator's purpose, timing, and addressed audience
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person narration may include an embedded or implied audience; the narrator may be conscious of telling the story to a given audience, perhaps at a given place and time, for a given reason. Why is this narrator telling the story in this way, why now, and are they to be trusted?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the narrator is writing privately (diary), to one person, to the public, or simply recounting memory. This affects voice, tone, structure, and the plausibility of knowledge. Make narrator's motive and context consistent and narratively useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person plural ('we')
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first-person-plural point of view, narrators tell the story using 'we' — no individual speaker is identified; the narrator is a member of a group that acts as a unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rare POV can increase group perspective or emphasize collective identity. Examples: Faulkner's experimentation, Jeffrey Eugenides' The Virgin Suicides. Use deliberately to create social/communal voice; be mindful of coherence and authority of the collective narrator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple or shifting first-person narrators
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person narrators can also be multiple, as in Ryūnosuke Akutagawa's In a Grove and Faulkner's The Sound and the Fury. Each source provides different accounts of the same event from the point of view of various first-person narrators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple narrators allow juxtaposing subjective accounts and highlighting contradictions. Make clear who narrates each section/chapter and avoid confusing the reader; ensure each voice is distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person omniscient (rare)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rare form of the first person is the first-person omniscient, in which the narrator is a character in the story, but also knows the thoughts and feelings of all the other characters. It can seem like third-person omniscient at times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form usually requires a plausible mechanic or explanation (e.g., supernatural vantage, death/post-mortem observation) to justify knowledge beyond the narrator's experience. Examples: The Book Thief (Death as narrator), The Lovely Bones. Use cautiously to avoid breaking reader trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms: interior monologue, dramatic monologue, and temporary first-person
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person narratives can appear in several forms; interior monologue (Notes from Underground), dramatic monologue (The Fall), or explicitly (Adventures of Huckleberry Finn). Other forms include temporary first-person narration as a story within a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a form that suits the story's aims: stream-of-consciousness for interiority, dramatic monologue for character confession, or temporary first-person for framed episodes. Be consistent and use form to shape pacing and access to thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and voice: mode of telling (written, spoken, thought) and its effects
rubrics_metrics.description: With a first-person narrative it is important to consider how the story is being told, i.e., is the character writing it down, telling it out loud, thinking it to themselves? And if they are writing it down, is it something meant to be read by the public, a private diary, or a story meant for one other person? The way the first-person narrator is relating the story will affect the language used, the length of sentences, the tone of voice, and many other things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match diction, syntax, and sentence length to the narrator's presumed mode and audience. A private diary may use short, raw sentences and intimate detail; a public memoir may be more polished. Consider stream-of-consciousness tendencies and the 'false document' device (diary, letters) for verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detective-fiction suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the narrator is within the story, he or she may not have knowledge of all the events. For this reason, the first-person narrative is often used for detective fiction, so that the reader and narrator uncover the case together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A common tactic is to use the detective's assistant (Watson) as narrator so clues and deductions unfold with plausible gaps. Use the narrator's limited knowledge to sustain mystery; avoid giving them secret omniscience that undermines suspense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-specific application: film and visual storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternatively, in a visual storytelling medium (such as video, television, or film), the first-person perspective is a graphical perspective rendered through a character's visual field, so the camera is 'seeing' out of a character's eyes. First-person narration is more difficult to achieve in film; however, voice-over narration can create the same structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In film, use visual POV shots or voice-over to approximate first-person voice. Be aware that film's visual omniscience can conflict with a strictly limited internal perspective; choose techniques (camera placement, selective information) to preserve the intended limitation.
